title: Arsenal announce season-ticket price increase, introduction of safe standing
content:
Arsenal have announced the introduction of safe standing at the Emirates Stadium from the 2026-27 season, alongside a series of ticketing changes that will see prices rise by an average of 3.9 percent for a general admission season ticket.

The implementation of safe standing represents the culmination of years of campaigning by supporters’ groups and extensive consultation carried out by the club.

A 2017 survey by the Arsenal Supporters’ Trust (AST) showed 96 percent of the fans to be in favour of safe standing. From next season, home and away supporters in the Clock End lower tier will benefit from safe standing rails. The season after, safe standing will be rolled out to the North Bank. By the 2027-28 season, there will be approximately 13,500 fans making use of the safe standing facilities.

The AST welcomed the introduction of safe standing after 10 years of campaigning.

“It shouldn’t have taken this long and some of the reasons Arsenal have put forward over the years for not introducing safe standing have been obstructive,” a statement read. “But we give credit to (CEO) Rich Garlick and his executive team who have recognised the importance of the issue to fans. Club and fans can now move forward together.”

Against a backdrop of rising costs, intense competition from wealthy clubs, and an unprecedented level of demand for tickets, Arsenal have opted to raise prices for a fifth consecutive year. Arsenal froze the majority of prices between 2014 and 2022, but have opted for incremental rises each year since then.

On average, prices for general admission and “Club Level” seats — Arsenal’s premium, mid-tier seating package — will increase by 3.9 percent.

“We are disappointed that the FSA’s ‘Protect the Fans, Protect the Game’ proposals calling for a ticket price freeze across all Premier League clubs has not been taken up. Neither the Premier League nor Arsenal have seriously engaged with the idea that a freeze at all clubs would help stop the ‘arms race’,” the AST said.

“We firmly believe that with the football sector benefitting from ever-increasing broadcast and commercial revenues it is time to stop squeezing match-going supporters so hard.

“We now expect both Arsenal and the Premier League to give more explanation as to why they have chosen to ignore the compelling case for a price freeze put forward by the ‘Protect the Fans, Protect the Game’ campaign, which was overwhelmingly backed by supporters including all representative members of the Arsenal Advisory Board (AAB).”

Earlier this season, The Athletic looked into the most expensive adult season tickets at each Premier League club. The below graphic shows this came in as £1,736 for Arsenal, putting them third behind Tottenham Hotspur and Fulham. With the increase, the new price for the same ticket at the Emirates will be £1,835.

The mechanism to achieve the greater revenue will be the introduction of two new match categories. Previously, Arsenal’s fixtures have been categorised by a three-tiered pricing strategy: Category A, Category B, and Category C.

From next season, Arsenal will introduce two new categories. “B+” will be used for two Premier League fixtures against teams outside of the traditional “big six” where there is a greater demand or significance — perhaps a Newcastle United or an Aston Villa. Category “A+” will be reserved for the home legs of any hypothetical Champions League quarter-final or semi-final.

That increase in cost will be partially offset by one of Arsenal’s four group-stage European games being reclassified as ‘Category C’.

Supporters will once again be able to choose between a 23-game season ticket, which includes Arsenal’s home group stage fixtures of European competition, and a 19-game ticket which includes Premier League home games only.

Arsenal also say they are protecting concessions for younger fans and senior supporters. The club will also be continuing their initiative to provide 1,000 free tickets for members of the local community.

No price hike is ever welcome among supporters.

Arsenal fans will naturally be disappointed to see prices increased again — but the huge demand for tickets, amplified by what promises to be a successful season, means the club will feel confident about their renewal rates. While the income achieved by a price rise may appear to be a relatively small percentage of Arsenal’s overall revenue, the club clearly feel the need to maximise every possible resource to remain competitive.

The decision to implement safe standing is much more positive news. Arsenal fans overwhelmingly wanted to see this introduced. Significant sections of the Clock End and North Bank lower tiers have been unofficially “safe standing” environments for years, but it’s good to see the club recognising and formalising that.

Arsenal have now followed the likes of Chelsea, Tottenham Hotspur, Liverpool, Manchester City and Manchester United in doing so.
